client: I got promoted at work a few weeks ago, and honestly, I thought I'd feel excited about it, but instead I just feel completely overwhelmed. Every day I go in and I'm surrounded by all these new responsibilities and I keep thinking, what if I'm not actually good enough for this role? I'm not even sure talking about it is going to change anything, because the pressure is real and it's not just going to disappear because I understand it better.
therapist: What you're describing — that gap between expecting excitement and feeling overwhelmed instead — makes a lot of sense, and it's actually really common when we step into something that stretches us. That thought, *"what if I'm not actually good enough,"* sounds like it's carrying a lot of weight for you right now. I'm also curious — even as you're describing all this pressure, there's something in how you're speaking that feels almost quieter, more subdued than the urgency of the situation; I wonder if underneath the overwhelm, there might also be some exhaustion or doubt about whether you even deserve to feel supported right now?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: Yeah, I think you're onto something with the exhaustion part, but the "deserving support" thing feels a bit off to me, like I don't think it's that deep. It's more that I just feel like I should be handling this on my own, because I was the one who wanted the promotion in the first place, so it feels almost embarrassing to admit I'm struggling with it. Like, I made my bed and now I have to lie in it, you know?
therapist: That belief — "I made my bed, now I lie in it" — is such a common but quietly punishing way of thinking, because it essentially says that wanting something means you forfeit the right to find it hard. I'm curious, would you apply that same logic to someone else you cared about — if a friend got a promotion they'd worked hard for and then struggled, would you tell them they should just handle it alone and be embarrassed about it? It might be worth gently examining whether the standard you're holding yourself to is actually as fair as it feels.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I mean, no, obviously I wouldn't tell a friend that, I'd probably tell them it's okay to struggle and that it doesn't mean they made a mistake. But when I try to apply that same thinking to myself it just doesn't stick, it feels like I'm making excuses for myself rather than actually being kind. I don't know why it's so easy to see it one way for other people and then completely flip it when it's about me.
therapist: You've just spotted something really important — that double standard between how you treat others versus yourself — and the fact that you can see it so clearly suggests part of you already knows the self-compassion is valid, even if it doesn't *feel* valid yet. That word "excuses" is interesting though, because it implies you'd be getting away with something, and I'm curious what you think you'd actually be letting yourself off the hook for — what's the thing you feel you need to be held accountable to here?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, loud, very rapid speech

client: I think what I feel like I need to be accountable to is just... performing at the level they hired me for, like proving that the people who promoted me weren't wrong about me. And if I'm struggling and I let myself off the hook for that, it feels like I'm accepting that maybe I'm not capable, which is scarier than just pushing through and pretending I'm fine. I guess I've tied being accountable to never showing any weakness, and I can see how that's a bit of a trap, but I don't really know how to get out of it.
therapist: You've actually just done something really significant — you named the trap yourself, which takes real clarity and courage, and that's not nothing. What strikes me is that the very thing you're afraid of, being seen as not capable, is being reinforced by the strategy you're using to avoid it, because pushing through alone and pretending you're fine doesn't actually give you evidence that you *are* capable, it just delays the fear. I wonder what it might look like to redefine accountability not as "never struggling" but as "facing something hard and finding a way through it" — because by that measure, you're already doing it right now.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, very quiet, moderate-paced speech

client: That reframe actually does land a little differently, like I can almost see the logic in it, but I think my worry is that the people I work with aren't going to grade me on that same curve. Even if I privately tell myself that struggling is part of the process, they're still watching me and forming opinions, and I can't exactly walk into a meeting and say "I'm figuring it out" without losing credibility. So it helps a bit internally, but it doesn't really solve the external pressure part.
therapist: That's a really valid distinction — the internal shift and the external reality are two genuinely different problems, and it makes sense that solving one doesn't automatically solve the other. I notice you're speaking quite quickly as you work through this, and I wonder if part of what's driving that urgency is that the external pressure feels very *live* for you right now, like it's not abstract at all. It might be worth exploring what evidence you actually have that your colleagues see you as struggling — because sometimes when we're watching ourselves this closely, we assume others are watching just as critically, and that assumption is worth testing.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: Honestly, if I'm being fair, I don't have concrete evidence that they think I'm failing, it's more just a feeling I carry into every meeting. But the thing is, absence of evidence isn't really reassuring to me, because I keep thinking they might just be polite or waiting to see how things unfold before they say anything. So testing that assumption sounds reasonable in theory, but I'm not sure how I'd actually do it without either coming across as fishing for reassurance or making people notice that I'm uncertain.
therapist: What you've just described is actually a really well-known cognitive pattern called "unfalsifiable thinking" — where you've set things up so that no evidence could ever fully reassure you, because even silence becomes proof of something ominous. That's an exhausting place to live, and it makes sense that it's wearing on you. Rather than seeking reassurance from others, which as you said risks a spiral, I'm curious whether we could look at building your sense of credibility from the inside — what would *you* need to see from yourself in a meeting to feel like you'd shown up capably, independent of how others reacted?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: That's actually a question I haven't really asked myself before, and when I sit with it I realize I don't have a clear answer, which is kind of unsettling. I think part of me has been so focused on how others are perceiving me that I've never really defined what "good enough" looks like from my own perspective. But I'm also a little worried that if I set my own internal standard, I'll just make it impossibly high and end up in the same trap from a different angle.
therapist: The fact that you don't have an answer yet isn't a problem — it's actually the most honest and useful thing you've said, because it means you've found the real work. And your worry about setting an impossibly high bar for yourself is really self-aware, because that pattern — perfectionism shifting its shape rather than disappearing — is exactly what we'd want to watch for. So I'm curious, if you were setting a standard that was genuinely fair rather than punishing, what's one small, concrete thing that would tell you "I handled that meeting well" — not perfectly, just well enough?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I think if I'm being honest, something like "I contributed at least one useful thing to the conversation" might be a fair bar, like I said something that moved the discussion forward rather than just nodding along. But even as I say it, I notice I'm already second-guessing it, thinking that one contribution isn't really enough for someone in my position. I guess I can see that the perfectionism is doing exactly what you said it would, just reshaping itself, but knowing that doesn't automatically make it easier to hold the lower bar without feeling like I'm settling.
therapist: You just caught perfectionism red-handed in real time, which is actually a really meaningful moment — you set a fair bar, watched your mind immediately move the goalposts, and named it yourself. That gap between *knowing* the pattern and *feeling* okay with the lower bar is completely normal, because insight and emotional comfort tend to move at different speeds. I'm curious, when you imagine actually walking out of a meeting where you contributed one useful thing, what does the version of you that *isn't* second-guessing feel — even if it's just for a second?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: When I actually try to imagine that version of me, there's something that feels almost like relief, like I could just exhale for a second instead of immediately scanning for what I did wrong. It's a small feeling but it's there, and I think that's actually what I'm chasing without realizing it, just a moment of feeling like I did okay. The hard part is that it feels almost dangerous to let myself feel that, like if I relax even briefly I'll miss something important and that's when things will fall apart.
therapist: That moment of relief you described — that exhale — that's not a small thing, that's actually your nervous system telling you what it's been needing all along. What strikes me is that even as you're describing something that sounds almost peaceful, there's an energy in how you're speaking, quite fast and heightened, like part of you is already bracing against that relief before you've even fully let it in. That belief that relaxing is dangerous, that it's the moment things fall apart, is worth sitting with — because it suggests your vigilance has been working so hard to protect you that it's never learned it's safe to rest, even briefly.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: I think you're right that the vigilance has been there for a long time, it's not just about this promotion, it's kind of how I've operated for years, always waiting for the thing I missed to catch up with me. But when you say it's never learned it's safe to rest, I don't really know how you teach it that, because it's not like I can just decide to feel safe and have that be enough. It feels like you're describing a solution that makes sense intellectually but the actual mechanism for getting there is still really unclear to me.
therapist: You're absolutely right that you can't just decide to feel safe — that would be like telling someone with a fear of heights to simply choose not to be afraid, and it misses the reality of how deeply embedded this pattern is. What I notice is that even as you're asking this question quite calmly and logically, there's something in your voice that sounds almost urgent, like this isn't just an intellectual curiosity but something that really matters to you to figure out — and I think that urgency itself is worth acknowledging, because it tells me this isn't abstract for you at all. The mechanism, if it helps to hear it, isn't a single decision but something more like collecting small pieces of evidence over time that the thing you missed *didn't* catch up with you — and that exhale you described earlier might actually be one of the first places to start.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech
